old: And when this has been said, one should not think that heaviness and lightness in a substance are of no account; for light substances abound in the qualities of air (vāyu) and fire (agni), and the others abound in the qualities of earth and soma. Therefore light substances, even by their own quality, are by nature kindlers of the fire, and are said to be of little harm even when taken to satiety; heavy substances, however, are not by nature kindlers of the fire, because of dissimilarity, and hence, taken to satiety in excess, they are harmful, except with strength from exercise and of the fire. This is the measure that depends on the strength of the fire.
new: And when this has been said, one should not think that heaviness and lightness in a substance are of no account; for light substances abound in the qualities of air (vāyu) and fire (agni), and the others abound in the qualities of earth and soma. Therefore light substances, even by their own quality, are by nature kindlers of the fire, and are said to be of little harm even when taken to satiety; heavy substances, however, are not by nature kindlers of the fire, because of dissimilarity, and hence, taken to satiety, they are excessively harmful, except where there is strength from exercise and strength of the fire. This is the measure that depends on the strength of the fire.
why: reviewer (minor): atimātram most naturally qualifies doṣavanti ('excessively harmful'), since sauhityopayuktāni already says 'taken to satiety'; 'taken to satiety in excess' doubles the excess. 'except with strength from exercise and of the fire' is unclear English.
